[PURPOSE]: To compare the diagnostic performance of 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT and mpMRI for pelvic lymph node staging prior to radical prostatectomy in prostate cancer (PCa) patients based on per patient data.
[METHODS]: PubMed and Embase databases were searched until October 2020 for eligible studies evaluating head-to-head comparison of 68Ga-PSMA-PET/CT and mpMRI for the detection of pelvic lymph node metastases (PLNMs) using pelvic lymph node dissection (PLND) as gold standard. The pooled sensitivity, specificity, and area under the summary receiver-operating characteristics curve (AUC) were determined for the two imaging modalities.
[RESULTS]: Nine studies with 640 patients were included. The pooled sensitivity, specificity, and AUC for 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT vs. mpMRI were 0.71 (95% CI: 0.48-0.86) vs. 0.40 (95% CI: 0.16-0.71), 0.92 (95% CI: 0.88-0.95) vs. 0.92 (95% CI: 0.80-0.97), and 0.92 (95% CI: 0.88-0.95) vs. 0.82 (95% CI: 0.79-0.86), respectively. There was substantial heterogeneity for both imaging modalities, and meta-regression analysis revealed that the number of patients, prevalence of PLNMs, PSA level, reference standard, and risk classification might be the potential causes of heterogeneity.
[CONCLUSION]: This meta-analysis of head-to-head comparison studies confirms that there is a trend toward a higher sensitivity and diagnostic accuracy of 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT compared to mpMRI for the detection of PLNMs in PCa patients. Nevertheless, according to current guidelines, PLND still needs to be recommended in case of negative results from 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT due to significant risk of malignancy.

key_findings.finding: The strongest pooled evidence supports limited sensitivity rather than no value: a 2016 diagnostic meta-analysis of 75 studies/9,796 patients using prostatectomy pathology found MRI sensitivity/specificity of 57%/91% for extracapsular extension (ECE/T3a), 58%/96% for seminal-vesicle invasion (SVI/T3b), and 61%/88% for overall T3 disease. The authors concluded that MRI has high specificity but poor and heterogeneous sensitivity; 3-T and functional sequences only modestly improved sensitivity.

key_findings.finding: A 2023 real-world single-institution plus Pennsylvania regional-collaborative study directly supports the claim that mpMRI alone is insufficient for routine staging. Against prostatectomy pathology, institutional/community sensitivity across pT2N0, ECE, SVI, lymph-node involvement and bladder-neck invasion was only 2.9%-49.2% and 16.8%-24.4%, respectively; specificity was much better (89.1%-100% and 93.9%-98.6%). Accuracy was associated with clinical risk stratum, not MRI institution, 1.5 versus 3 T strength, or MRI timing; the authors advised against using mpMRI as the sole staging method.

key_findings.finding: For lymph-node staging specifically, a 2021 head-to-head meta-analysis of 9 studies/640 patients using pelvic lymph-node dissection as the reference standard found mpMRI pooled sensitivity 0.40 (95% CI 0.16-0.71), specificity 0.92 (0.80-0.97), and AUC 0.82 (0.79-0.86). Thus a negative mpMRI cannot reliably exclude nodal disease; PSMA PET/CT performed better for sensitivity (0.71) while retaining specificity 0.92, although even negative PSMA imaging did not eliminate the need for PLND in guideline-based care.

source_tools.relevance: Direct pooled nodal accuracy against PLND pathology

key_findings.finding: Recent multicenter evidence confirms the SVI limitation: among 528 prostatectomy patients, 86 had SVI on final pathology; MRI sensitivity was only 0.162 (95% CI 0.088-0.261) with specificity 0.963 (0.940-0.979). This pattern means MRI-positive SVI is relatively credible, but MRI misses most pathologic SVI.

source_tools.relevance: Multicenter contemporary mpMRI study with prostatectomy pathology reference

key_findings.finding: Overall stage agreement can be clinically meaningful but is imperfect and highly dependent on image quality: a 2023 multicenter European study found MRI T stage exactly matched prostatectomy pathology in 71.2% of cases; nondiagnostic/poor-quality scans (PI-QUAL <3) had more pathological upstaging (35% vs 19% for PI-QUAL >=3; OR 3.4, p=0.01). This refutes the absolute claim that mpMRI provides little information in every setting, while demonstrating substantial under-staging when image quality is poor.

Evidence for routine clinical impact is weak or negative. In a randomized 438-patient trial (2015), preoperative MRI did not significantly reduce positive surgical margins overall: 19% versus 23% without MRI (p=0.4), although a cT1 subgroup showed a possible benefit (16% vs 27%, p=0.035). In a 2023 propensity-weighted cohort of 1,259 prostatectomy patients, mpMRI versus CT produced no significant difference in positive-margin rate (OR 1.03, 95% CI 0.77-1.38), biochemical-recurrence-free survival (HR 1.21, 0.84-1.74), complications, or 1-year functional outcomes.

The balanced conclusion is that the claim is substantially supported if it means 'mpMRI is not sufficiently accurate to replace pathology, nomograms, or risk-adapted surgical/lymph-node staging in routine practice,' especially because sensitivity is poor for microscopic/focal ECE, SVI, and nodal disease. It is overstated if it means 'mpMRI has no clinically useful information': high specificity can confirm gross locally advanced disease, MRI can help side/extent-of-disease and operative planning in selected patients, and performance improves with high-quality 3-T functional imaging and expert interpretation. The evidence base is also limited by retrospective designs, heterogeneous protocols/readers, selection and referral bias, and pathology-based cohorts enriched for surgery candidates.
